common_name: Adams II Elderberry (Adams No. 2, Large-Fruited Union Springs American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; although Adams No. 2 sets some fruit on its own, planting it alongside Adams No. 1 (the original companion selection) or another distinct American elderberry cultivar such as Nova or York substantially increases fruit set and cluster size.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Adams No. 2 is one of two wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) selections made by grower William Adams near Union Springs, New York in 1915; the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva trialed the seedling alongside its sibling Adams No. 1 for eleven years before releasing both as named cultivars in 1926. Until improved mid-century releases such as York and Kent arrived, the two Adams selections were essentially the only named elderberry cultivars grown commercially in North America, and Adams No. 2 in particular became known for producing the largest individual berries of any named American elderberry, borne in broad, flat-topped cymes up to six inches across. Flowers open in June–July and the small, dark purple-black berries ripen late, from late August into September, over an extended four-week picking window. As with all elderberry, raw fruit contains cyanogenic glycosides and must be cooked before eating; the ripe berries are used for elderberry syrup, wine, jelly, and juice, and the flower clusters can be battered and fried or steeped for elderflower cordial. Like other American elderberry, it spreads by root suckers and benefits from removing the oldest canes each winter to keep the planting productive.
